homepageFaq.question: What scale is Warhammer 40k miniatures?
homepageFaq.answer: Most people in the hobby treat Games Workshop miniatures as 32mm heroic scale, measured from eye level at roughly 160cm. To convert from true 28mm, scale your STL to 114.3% in your slicer. Your mileage may vary depending on the sculpt.

homepageFaq.question: How do I convert 28mm to 32mm for D&D?
homepageFaq.answer: Multiply your 28mm STL file by 114.3% to get what most players call heroic 32mm scale. This accounts for the 175cm human baseline and eye-level measurement I use on STLACCESS. If your group uses something different, adjust accordingly.

homepageFaq.question: Does material shrinkage affect FDM miniatures?
homepageFaq.answer: PLA and PETG shrink about 0.2-0.5% during cooling. This is small enough that I do not add compensation. If you want maximum accuracy, print a test piece first and measure with calipers.

homepageFaq.question: What is the difference between 28mm and 32mm miniatures?
homepageFaq.answer: 28mm true scale measures a 175cm human from eye level. 32mm heroic scale uses the same baseline but adds exaggerated proportions for detail and durability. A 32mm miniature ends up roughly 14% taller than its 28mm equivalent.
homepageFaq.answerExtra: Games Workshop uses 32mm heroic for Warhammer 40k. A lot of D&D and Pathfinder miniatures are closer to 28mm true scale, though it varies by manufacturer.

homepageFaq.question: How do I scale an STL file in my slicer?
homepageFaq.answer: Import the STL into your slicer (Chitubox, Lychee, PrusaSlicer, or Cura). Select the model, open the scale tool, and enter the percentage from the STL scale calculator. Lock the X, Y, and Z axes to uniform scaling. Apply the change and slice as normal.

homepageFaq.question: What does 1:56 scale mean in miniature gaming?
homepageFaq.answer: 1:56 is a ratio scale common in historical wargaming, including Bolt Action. It works out to roughly 28mm true scale when you use a 175cm human baseline. To convert 1:56 STLs to 32mm heroic, most people scale them to 114.3%.

referencePageQA.question: What percentage do I scale 28mm to 32mm?
referencePageQA.answer: Type 114.3% into your slicer. That is the number for 28mm to 32mm measured to eye level. If you measure to the top of the head instead, use 116.1%. I have tested this on PLA with no additional shrinkage compensation needed.

referencePageQA.question: How big is a 28mm miniature in real measurements?
referencePageQA.answer: A 28mm miniature represents a 175cm human at roughly 1:56 to 1:60 ratio scale. The miniature stands about 30-32mm to the top of the head, with the eye level at 28mm. Add 2-5mm for the base thickness and you have the total height sitting on your table.

referencePageQA.question: What is the difference between 28mm and 32mm scale?
referencePageQA.answer: 28mm is the classic tabletop standard — measured to eye level on a 175cm human with realistic proportions. 32mm heroic scale uses the same baseline but exaggerates heads, hands, and weapons so details read at arm's length. The height difference is only 14.3%, but the added bulk makes them feel a lot bigger on the table. Full conversion guide

referencePageQA.question: What scale is 1:35 in mm for miniatures?
referencePageQA.answer: At 1:35, a 175cm human works out to about 50mm to the eyes. That is significantly bigger than 28mm tabletop miniatures — most 1:35 kits are Tamiya-style military models, not wargaming miniatures. If you want to mix a 1:35 tank with 28mm infantry, scale it down to 62.5% in your slicer.

referencePageQA.question: Does PLA or PETG shrink after printing?
referencePageQA.answer: Barely. PLA and PETG can shrink 0.2% to 0.5% as they cool from printing temperature. This is small enough to ignore for miniature scaling. I do not add compensation for FDM because over-extrusion and cooling shrinkage tend to cancel each other out.

referencePageQA.question: Why do 1:48 tanks look better with 28mm infantry than 1:56?
referencePageQA.answer: Here is the thing — most modern 28mm plastics from Warlord Games and similar manufacturers actually measure closer to 30-32mm. A true 1:56 tank looks undersized next to them. 1:48 Tamiya kits match the heroic proportions better, and they are often cheaper than official wargaming vehicles. I use 1:48 for my Bolt Action motor pool and nobody has complained at tournaments. Use my 1:48 to 28mm guide and see how it looks on your table.

referencePageQA.question: What does "Eye Level" vs "Top of Head" mean in miniature scale?
referencePageQA.answer: Eye level means measuring from the foot to the centre of the eye — 160cm on a 175cm human. Top of head means measuring to the crown at 175cm. That 15cm gap creates a 5-10% difference in your scale calculations. Fantasy and sci-fi miniatures usually use eye level because helmets and top-knots vary. Historical kits tend to use top of head. The STL scale converter supports both.

referencePageQA.question: How do I scale STL files for different tabletop games?
referencePageQA.answer: Find your source and target scales in the conversion details below, type the percentage into your slicer, and lock the XYZ axes to uniform scaling. Always print a test piece before committing to a full batch. The STL scale calculator on the homepage does this automatically — pick your scales, copy the number, done.
